newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austria far right says no coalition before polls.
newsitem.headline: Austria far right says no coalition before polls.

text.p: Austrian far-right leader Joerg Haider said on Thursday his party would not rush into a coalition with the conservatives and denied the two parties had recently held talks over forming a government.

Haider, whose nationalist Freedom Party scored nearly 28 percent in European elections last October, insisted fresh elections had to be held before he would consider joining another party in a coalition.
"My position is that there will be no fleeting (government) changeover," Haider told a news conference.
"Only if the coalition collapsed would we be prepared to support a minority government for a couple of months in the transition period ahead of fresh elections," he added.
Haider was holding his first news conference since chancellor Franz Vranitzky resigned on Saturday and named finance minister Viktor Klima as his successor.

Haider denied reports in the Austrian media that informal coalition talks were held by telephone over the weekend between a member of his party and an official of the conservative People's Party following Vranitzky's resignation.
A People's Party spokesman, who wished to remain anonymous, told Reuters that such a discussion had taken place.
Asked if the reports were lies, Haider said: "Yes".
"The People's Party constantly want something from us, but I'm not prepared to go for it," he said.

Haider attacked People's Party leader Foreign Minister Wolfgang Schuessel for what he called his "clumsy hesitation" over the sale two weeks ago of the flagship bank Creditanstalt to the Social Democrat-favoured candidate Bank Austria.
Schuessel had paved the way for the phoenix-like rise of chancellor-designate Klima, Haider said.
Klima is putting together a new cabinet and shaking up the ministerial portfolios among his Social Democrats, with indications that leftwingers are being ousted from top posts in favour of moderates.
Adopting a more centrist line is likely to stabilise the coalition with the conservatives, but the partnership is still considered to be an uneasy one.

After announcing his resignation, Vranitzky categorically ruled out any chance of a partnership between the far right and the Social Democrats. Schuessel has also said he would not join a coalition with Haider.
The Freedom Party and the conservatives would currently be able to command a majority in parliament and have voted together on a number of issues to block the Social Democrats.
Vranitzky expressed regret in a valedictory news conference on Sunday that his party had failed to react quickly enough to the fast-growing popularity of the far-right.

While the Social Democrat vote has slumped since Vranitzky took over in 1986 -- dipping below 30 percent in the October Euro-poll -- support for the far right has risen sharply from around nine percent ten years ago before Haider became leader.
